findings.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £67k if 3.3% uplift accepted against 3% budget assumption
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget assumed 3% pay inflation, but National Employers offered 3.3% on 2 June 2026. The offer remains unaccepted by unions. If accepted, the council quantifies the additional cost as 'around £67k' for the year.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pay inflation is a direct hit to the bottom line with no mitigation identified; represents unfunded cost pressure.
findings.figures: £67k impact if 3.3% accepted; 0.3 percentage point difference from budgeted 3%
findings.quote: If this pay award is accepted later, the overall impact on the budget for the year would be around £67k.

findings.headline: Stapleford Towns Fund street improvement scheme flagged with explicit budget risk to completion
findings.detail: Early 2027 completion target with project designs underway and public consultation in September. The council explicitly notes that 'budget remains a risk until completion,' suggesting the full scope or timeline could drive costs above the allocated budget within the multi-year scheme.
findings.matters: Acknowledged budget risk on externally-funded scheme affects council's ability to deliver town regeneration commitments within available funding.
findings.figures: Part of Stapleford Towns Fund (£5.713m approved), target completion early 2027
findings.quote: Project to complete early 2027, although budget remains a risk until completion.

findings.headline: Housing structural repairs budget at risk due to legacy issues and case volumes
findings.detail: At 28% spend in Q1 (£56k of £200k), the council flags 'some risk with budget due to number of cases and legacy issues.' Legacy property defects are harder to predict and potentially cost more than anticipated.
findings.matters: Structural defects are not discretionary spending; unbudgeted costs cannot be deferred and may force reductions elsewhere.
findings.figures: £200k budget, £56k spent to 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Structural Remedial Repairs: 200 56 In progress. Some risk with budget due to number of cases and legacy issues.

findings.headline: Housing damp proofing programme 50% spent by end of Q1 with acknowledged budget risk
findings.detail: The damp proofing works have consumed £75k of a £150k annual budget in just three months, with the council noting risk 'with half of budget already spent.' This pace of spending suggests potential year-end budget exhaustion.
findings.matters: Rapid budget consumption in Q1 signals potential underfunding of housing condition works, requiring scope reduction or additional allocation mid-year.
findings.figures: £150k budget, £75k spent (50%), within first three months of financial year
findings.quote: Damp Proofing Works: 150 75 In progress. Some risks with half of budget already spent.

findings.headline: Brinsley Headstocks refurbishment costs flagged as likely to exceed £137k budget
findings.detail: The procurement stage for this scheme is in its final stage, with the council explicitly noting that costs are likely to exceed the approved budget. No spend has yet occurred in Q1.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on approved capital schemes require finding additional funding or cutting other priorities, affecting overall capital delivery.
findings.figures: £137k budget, £0 spent to 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Refurbishment of Brinsley Headstocks: 137 - Final stage of procurement underway, costs are likely to exceed budget.

findings.paper_title: Statement of Accounts Update and Outturn Position 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA deficit driven by both rising costs and falling rent income, with no immediate recovery plan detailed
findings.detail: The paper attributes the HRA deterioration to 'an accumulation of rising costs over several years and lower than anticipated rent incomes being received in 2025/26'. An HRA Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Business Strategy is being developed to address this, but the paper does not detail specific interventions or timescales.
findings.matters: Sustained cost inflation combined with income below forecast suggests the HRA model is under structural pressure, not just a one-year variance. Without visible recovery steps, the trend is concerning.
findings.figures: HRA overspend £276k; working balance deficit £946k
findings.quote: This outturn position has resulted from an accumulation of rising costs over several years and lower than anticipated rent incomes being received in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Statement of Accounts Update and Outturn Position 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA Working Balance has fallen below the Section 151 Officer's minimum recommended level of £1 million
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account working balance stood at £946k as at 31 March 2026, below the £1m minimum. This follows a £276k overspend against revised estimates, driven by accumulating rising costs and lower-than-anticipated rent income in 2025/26. The council acknowledges this can be tolerated short-term but says sustained efforts are required to recover.
findings.matters: A working balance below minimum signals tightening cash flexibility and suggests the council is managing HRA pressures through reserve depletion rather than service adjustment or rent increases. For lenders, this indicates housing finances are under strain.
findings.figures: HRA Working Balance £946k as at 31 March 2026; minimum recommended level £1m; HRA overspend £276k against revised estimates
findings.quote: With the budget deficit being higher than anticipated, the HRA Working Balance has now dipped below the Section 151 Officer's minimum recommended level of £1 million.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Audit of Accounts and Associated Matters
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued C3 grade in January 2026, citing serious failings in consumer standards
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing assigned a C3 rating to Broxtowe citing serious failings in delivering consumer standards outcomes, with significant improvements required. The auditor has identified this as a risk indicating a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for the 2025-26 financial year.
findings.matters: A C3 regulatory rating signals governance and operational failures in the council's social housing management, raising material concerns about management capability and service delivery effectiveness.
findings.figures: C3 grade issued January 2026
findings.quote: In January 2026, The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grade for the Council, citing serious failings in the delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvements were needed.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates structural uncertainty with ongoing Government participation required
findings.detail: The council is participating in Government-directed Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) process. An internal LGR Implementation Group meets fortnightly and a dedicated reorganisation specialist officer has been appointed. The council is preparing for potential structural change but the outcome and timeline remain uncertain.
findings.matters: LGR represents fundamental uncertainty about the council's future structure, functions, funding arrangements, and viability; lenders must understand transition risks, potential effects on service continuity, and long-term ability to service debt.
findings.figures: 1 reorganisation specialist officer appointed; implementation group meets fortnightly
findings.quote: There is an internal Local Government Reorganisation Implementation Group that meets fortnightly and an Officer has been appointed as the Council's Reorganisation specialist.

findings.headline: Budget gap identified requiring financial strategy refresh and cost reduction actions
findings.detail: The council reviewed and refreshed its Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Business Strategy in November 2025 in response to identified financial challenges. The refreshed Business Strategy sets out required actions to reduce costs, generate additional income, and improve services. A forward-looking action plan includes another MTFS review with a target date of November 2026 to ensure the budget gap is managed at a sustainable level.
findings.matters: Budget gaps directly threaten financial sustainability and debt service capacity; a lender needs confidence that identified shortfalls have credible, fully-costed solutions—the timing (still working on it six months into the year) raises questions about execution.
findings.figures: Budget gap identified November 2025; gap management plan due November 2026
findings.quote: The Business Strategy identified the actions required to reduce costs, generate additional income and/or improve services in order to meet the financial challenges faced by the Council and to mitigate against any budget risks.

findings.headline: Chief Executive retired mid-year; interim leadership appointed while permanent recruitment underway
findings.detail: The council's long-standing Chief Executive retired during 2025/26. The council appointed an Interim Chief Executive, Interim Deputy Chief Executive, and three additional interim director-level appointments to maintain resilience. Permanent recruitment for the Chief Executive is in progress but not yet complete as of the governance statement date (May 2026).
findings.matters: Leadership continuity is critical during periods of financial stress and regulatory challenge; interim arrangements create governance and execution risks, particularly given the council is simultaneously addressing a budget gap and a housing regulator failure.
findings.figures: 1 chief executive retired; 4 interim senior positions created (1 chief executive, 1 deputy, 3 directors)
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council's long-standing Chief Executive retired. Full Council appointed an Interim Chief Executive and an Interim Deputy Chief Executive while the permanent recruitment process takes place.

findings.headline: Housing regulator inspection resulted in C3 rating with serious failings in fire safety and tenant needs
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing completed an inspection in October 2025 and rated Broxtowe C3, the worst rating under new assessment regulations introduced in 2023. The inspection identified two serious failings: fire safety management (unclear timelines on open actions, no evidence of mitigations in place), and inability to understand and tailor services to diverse tenant groups. The council is implementing a Service Improvement Plan to address these.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in a core housing service indicates operational and compliance weaknesses, exposes the council to reputational damage and remediation costs, and reflects governance gaps that could affect creditworthiness and lender confidence.
findings.figures: C3 rating; serious failings identified in 2 areas (fire safety, diverse needs); weaknesses also identified in data quality, performance reporting, complaints learning, and ASB/hate crime accessibility
findings.quote: Following the inspection, Broxtowe Borough Council has received a C3 rating from RSH, meaning that the Council is not meeting the Regulator's requirements and must work to improve its position.

findings.headline: Non-compliance with Regulator recommendations will carry formal consequences, with implementation required as soon as practicable
findings.detail: The Head of Legal Services explicitly states that failure to adhere to the Regulator's recommendations will have consequences and emphasizes that implementation must occur as soon as practicably possible. This indicates active regulatory enforcement powers beyond the improvement plan itself.
findings.matters: This signals that non-compliance with the improvement plan carries formal regulatory penalties, making the compliance deadline material and urgent
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Failure to adhere to the recommendations of the Regulator will have consequences. It is imperative that the Regulators recommendations are considered and implemented as soon as practicably possible.

findings.headline: The council faces potential future compliance costs from the Regulator's requirements, with scale unknown and requiring cabinet approval if they exceed current resources
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer confirms there are currently no financial implications to the Housing Revenue Account from the C3 rating. However, the statement explicitly reserves that any future cost uplift from compliance work that cannot be absorbed within existing resources will require Cabinet approval, indicating potential financial exposure.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need visibility of potential costs from regulatory compliance, even if currently unquantified, as they could affect HRA budget flexibility
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There are no financial implications to consider for the Housing Revenue Account at this stage. Any uplift in costs going forward that cannot be contained within existing resources would require approval by Cabinet.

findings.headline: Broxtowe received a C3 rating from the Regulator of Social Housing for failing to meet consumer standards
findings.detail: Following an inspection in October 2025, the first assessment under the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023, Broxtowe received a C3 rating from RSH. This means the council is not meeting regulatory requirements and must work to improve. The Regulator noted constructive engagement but made clear that improvement is required.
findings.matters: A regulatory failure is a material governance issue that signals potential systemic problems in housing service delivery and could affect the council's standing as a regulated provider
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Following the inspection, the Council has received a C3 rating from RSH, meaning that the Council is not meeting the Regulator's requirements and must work to improve its position.

findings.headline: Pension actuarial valuation in March 2028 will reset employer contributions from 2029/30, with risk of increase coinciding with reserves crisis
findings.detail: The pension fund is currently fully funded at 105% and employer contributions have reduced to 16.8% of salary. However, the next actuarial valuation (March 2028) will set new contribution rates for 2029/30—precisely when the council's reserves are forecast to be critically depleted.
findings.matters: Any increase in pension contributions directly reduces available budget. A valuation change requiring higher contributions would hit the council at the moment it has minimal reserves to absorb the cost.
findings.figures: Current employer primary contribution 16.8% (down from 19.0%); next valuation March 2028 for 2029/30 implementation
findings.quote: The Pension Fund continues to perform well, with the Broxtowe element now fully funded at 105%. This may change again at the next actuarial valuation in March 2028 which will identify the employer's pension contributions required from 2029/30.

findings.headline: Capital receipts are assumed to materialise but remain uncertain; failure would threaten capital programme viability and force additional borrowing
findings.detail: The MTFS financing depends on assumed capital receipts (from asset sales). The document warns that if these do not materialise, the council will need to fund infrastructure from other resources or borrowing, with potential 'significant impact on the viability of the MTFS'.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are volatile and dependent on market conditions; if assets cannot be sold as forecast, either capital schemes are delayed (reducing service resilience) or the council increases borrowing (reducing financial flexibility).
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing of £3.0m proposed for 2026/27; no quantified capital receipts target disclosed
findings.quote: Should anticipated capital receipts not materialise, the Council will need to fund its infrastructure, including any new construction projects, fleet vehicles, maintenance and development of ICT systems and key assets, from other resources. This may have a significant impact on the viability of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Annual revenue deficits accelerate from £760k to £2.28m over the MTFS period, widening the structural imbalance
findings.detail: The council's annual deficits—the gap between budgeted expenditure and available income—grow substantially and persistently from 2026/27 onwards. By 2029/30 the annual deficit has tripled, indicating the Business Strategy frontloads easier savings while future years require progressively larger interventions.
findings.matters: Accelerating deficits indicate an unsustainable trajectory; the widening gap suggests the council cannot close the structural funding gap with current policy.
findings.quote: PLANNED (SURPLUS)/DEFICIT AFTER MOVEMENT IN RESERVES TO BE FUNDED FROM GENERAL FUND BALANCE: 760 / 1,246 / 1,908 / 2,280

findings.headline: Leisure facilities are reaching end-of-life and creating increasing capital budget pressure, with strategy review underway
findings.detail: The council's leisure facilities, managed through Liberty Leisure Limited, are ageing and placing 'increasing pressures on capital budgets'. The council is currently reviewing its Leisure Facilities Strategy to determine the way forward.
findings.matters: Aging leisure infrastructure typically requires substantial capital expenditure to replace or refurbish; timing and cost of these decisions will materially affect capital programme and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: Further challenges exist as the facilities through which leisure service operates are reaching the end-of-life stage and are placing increasing pressures on capital budgets. The Council is reviewing its Leisure Facilities Strategy, in order to develop a way forward for leisure services provision across Broxtowe.

findings.headline: Central government funding faces high risk from Fair Funding Review and Business Rates reset; outstanding rates appeals create further uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's funding is highly exposed to the Fair Funding Review outcome and Business Rates Retention Scheme reset. Outstanding rates appeals by businesses create material but unquantifiable uncertainty: the council acknowledges it is 'a challenge to come up with a meaningful estimate as to the level of rate reductions'.
findings.matters: Government funding and business rates are core income; volatility in these sources directly affects ability to balance without further reserve drawdown, and the council cannot control or predict outcomes.
findings.figures: Business Rates Baseline Funding Level drops from £4.610m (2025/26) to £2.995m (2026/27); Revenue Support Grant drops from £4.791m (2026/27) to £3.4m (2027/28 onwards)
findings.quote: The re-set of the Business Rates Retention Scheme has highlighted risks and vulnerability that local authorities face for reasons which are outside of their control.

findings.headline: Business Strategy savings and income proposals are still being developed with implementation risk, yet are essential to prevent reserve collapse
findings.detail: The council's budget balance depends entirely on unfinalized Business Strategy proposals. The document explicitly states these proposals are 'still being developed and finalised and may carry some implementation risk'. Without these, the council falls into negative reserves.
findings.matters: Implementation risk on core savings means the MTFS is contingent on uncertain delivery; a lender must understand which savings are firm versus speculative.
findings.figures: Not quantified by proposal; aggregate delivered into base budget figures
findings.quote: Members will be aware that some savings or income proposals are still being developed and finalised and may carry some implementation risk which could have an impact on the savings or income profile. It is essential for the financial health of the Council over the medium term that these efficiencies and additional income are achieved.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves fall to zero by 2029/30 on current trajectory, leaving no contingency buffer
findings.detail: The council's General Fund reserves are forecast to decline from £4.215m (March 2026) to £300k by end of 2028/29, then into negative territory (-£1.979m) in 2029/30. The council's s151 officer advises minimum reserves should be £1.5m; available reserves therefore drop to -£1.2m in 2028/29 and -£3.479m in 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty the council can weather unexpected events; reserves at these levels indicate the council is structurally insolvent unless all savings execute perfectly.
findings.figures: Opening £4.215m; closing 2028/29 £300k; closing 2029/30 -£1,979k. Minimum advised £1.5m. Available reserves 2028/29 -£1,200k; 2029/30 -£3,479k.
findings.quote: If all the assumptions as set out in this MTFS arise, and no further action is taken with regards to Business Strategy proposals, then overall reserve levels will reduce to just £300k by the end of 2028/29 and the fall into a negative position during 2029/30 and beyond.

findings.headline: Bramcote Crematorium income (£450k annually) is at risk if performance targets fail
findings.detail: The council receives an annual distribution from its joint ownership of Bramcote Crematorium with Erewash Borough Council. The 2026/27 distribution is budgeted at £450k. However, the strategy explicitly warns that 'any failure by the Crematorium to meet its targets for 2025/26 will be reflected in the distribution for 2026/27,' flagging income volatility tied to operational performance.
findings.matters: A £450k income stream is meaningful; the explicit performance caveat signals that budgeted income may not materialise if crematorium operations falter
findings.figures: Distribution to Broxtowe 2026/27: £450k
findings.quote: Any failure by the Crematorium to meet its targets for 2025/26 will be reflected in the distribution for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to fall 55% from £997k to £450k as cash balances and rates decline
findings.detail: The council forecasts investment interest income (less costs) will drop from £997k in 2024/25 to £450k in 2026/27. This reflects both lower interest rates and the drawdown of the investment base. The weighted average investment balance is forecast to fall from £21,580k to £13,000k. This materially reduces non-service revenue available to support council operations.
findings.matters: A 55% reduction in investment income is a significant loss of discretionary revenue; combined with reserve drawdown, it signals tighter financial flexibility
findings.figures: Total Interest 2024/25: £997k; Total Interest 2026/27: £450k; Weighted Average Total Investments 2024/25: £21,580k; 2026/27: £13,000k
findings.quote: Weighted Average Total Investments 21,580 [2024/25] ... 13,000 [2026/27]; Total Interest (less costs) 997 [2024/25] ... 450 [2026/27]; Rate of Return 4.62% [2024/25] ... 3.46% [2026/27]

findings.headline: Investment balances declining sharply from £21m to £10m as regeneration capital schemes reach completion
findings.detail: Total investment exposure is forecast to drop from £21,151k at 31 March 2026 to £12,000k at 31 March 2027, then plateau at £10,000k. The council explicitly attributes this to 'large capital grant funded regeneration schemes nearing completion and therefore the cash balances held for these schemes being fully applied.' This represents a one-time event that permanently reduces the council's liquidity buffer by roughly half.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial strength through cash reserves; this signals lower financial headroom from 2027/28 onwards to cover unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls
findings.figures: Investments 1 April 2025: £21,151k; Investments 31 March 2027: £12,000k; Investments 31 March 2028–2029: £10,000k
findings.quote: it is expected that investment balances will be substantially lower by the end of the current financial year and then levels off into future years. This is due to large capital grant funded regeneration schemes nearing completion and therefore the cash balances held for these schemes being fully applied.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Regulator of Social Housing - judgement document
findings.headline: Intensive regulatory monitoring ahead with enforcement powers under review
findings.detail: The regulator has committed to intensive engagement with Broxtowe and will keep enforcement powers under review. While enforcement is not being used immediately, it remains a possibility as the council works through its improvement plan.
findings.matters: Escalation to enforcement action would represent a material governance escalation affecting borrowing eligibility and credit risk perception.
findings.figures: No specific figures
findings.quote: Our engagement will be intensive, and we will seek assurance that Broxtowe BC is making sufficient progress, including ongoing monitoring of how it delivers its improvement plan. Our priority will be that risks to tenants are adequately managed and mitigated. We are not proposing to use our enforcement powers at this stage but will keep this under review as Broxtowe BC seeks to resolve these issues.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Regulator of Social Housing - judgement document
findings.headline: Stock condition survey backlog: only 63% of homes surveyed in last 18 months, 100% completion target end of 2026
findings.detail: Broxtowe does not have accurate and up-to-date information on the quality of all its tenants' homes. Only 63% of homes have had stock condition surveys completed in the last 18 months. The council has an accelerated programme to complete 100% surveys by end of 2026.
findings.matters: The survey backlog suggests unidentified capital needs in the housing stock and implies significant spend will be required in the accelerated completion programme through 2026.
findings.figures: 63% of homes having a stock condition survey completed in the last 18 months; 100% target by end of 2026
findings.quote: Broxtowe BC does not currently have accurate and up to date information on the quality of all of its tenants' homes (including any potential hazards in homes), with 63% of homes having a stock condition survey completed in the last 18 months. Its target is to complete 100% of surveys by the end of 2026, following an accelerated programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Regulator of Social Housing - judgement document
findings.headline: Over 3,000 overdue fire safety remedial actions across housing stock
findings.detail: Broxtowe has identified more than 3,000 overdue fire remedial actions, though most are assessed as medium risk. There is a lack of clarity about how long actions have been open and insufficient evidence of mitigations in place while these remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Fire safety compliance gaps represent both a tenant safety liability and a material financial liability requiring urgent capital expenditure to remediate.
findings.figures: more than 3,000 overdue fire remedial actions; most assessed as medium risk
findings.quote: Broxtowe BC had more than 3,000 overdue fire remedial actions. Although most actions were assessed as medium risk, there was a lack of clarity about the length of time they had been open, as well as a lack of evidence of mitigations in place while these actions remain outstanding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Regulator of Social Housing - judgement document
findings.headline: First C3 regulatory grade issued to Broxtowe for serious failings in consumer standards
findings.detail: The regulator has graded Broxtowe C3 for the first time, indicating serious failings in delivering consumer standards outcomes and that significant improvement is needed. The grade reflects failures in Safety and Quality Standards and Transparency, Influence and Accountability. Regulatory engagement will be intensive with enforcement powers under review.
findings.matters: A C3 grade indicates material regulatory risk and potential enforcement action, which could affect the council's borrowing capacity, credit terms, and stakeholder confidence.
findings.figures: C3 grade (first time issued); 4,415 social housing homes
findings.quote: we have concluded that there are serious failings in Broxtowe BC delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed

findings.headline: HRA housing acquisitions (£1.4m per annum) assume rental income will cover new borrowing costs
findings.detail: The HRA plans to acquire former right-to-buy and other properties at £1.4m per annum over the three-year period. The strategy assumes rental income from these acquisitions will be sufficient to cover the accompanying borrowing costs, but this is not guaranteed and carries risk if void periods or management costs erode the margin.
findings.matters: If actual rental income falls short of the assumed coverage, the HRA would need to cover shortfalls from revenue, further tightening an already constrained position and adding pressure to its minimum working balance.
findings.figures: £1.4m per annum in property acquisitions planned 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: The three-year capital programme includes £1.4m per annum for the acquisition of former right to buy and other properties by the HRA as set out in the Housing Delivery Plan...It is anticipated that the rental income from the properties acquired will meet the accompanying ongoing borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Borrowing finances 57% of planned 2026/27 capital spending, with General Fund capital receipts forecast at zero
findings.detail: Of the £24.010m capital programme, £13.736m will be financed by borrowing. General Fund capital receipts drop from £266k in 2025/26 to zero from 2026/27 onwards, removing a source of flexible funding and making the council wholly dependent on borrowing and grants for capital.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on borrowing with no offsetting capital receipts means the council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) will continue growing, locking in future debt servicing costs. Zero capital receipts removes a source of flexibility if schemes need to be deferred.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital financing: borrowing £13.736m of £24.010m total. General Fund capital receipts: £669k (2024/25), £266k (2025/26), £0k (2026/27 onwards)
findings.quote: Borrowing makes up the largest proportion of the capital financing over the next three years.

findings.headline: Investment balances falling from £21.151m to £10.000m as grant-funded schemes complete
findings.detail: Large cash holdings tied up in grant-funded schemes (Towns Deal, Regeneration) are being drawn down as projects finish. Investment balances will drop by 53% and remain at the lower level, reducing both the liquidity buffer and investment income accruing to the council.
findings.matters: Lower cash reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or seasonal timing mismatches. Combined with rising financing costs, this creates less headroom to manage volatility without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £21.151m (2025/26), falling to £12.000m (2026/27), then £10.000m (2027/28–2028/29). Expected reduction 2025/26: £9.151m
findings.quote: As demonstrated above, it is expected that investment balances will be substantially lower by the end of the current financial year and into future years. This is due to large grant funded schemes, such as the Stapleford Towns Deal scheme, is nearing completion and therefore the grant balances associated with these schemes being fully allocated.

findings.headline: HRA can no longer fund capital from revenue without risking its minimum working balance
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account ceased making revenue contributions to capital financing in 2023/24 because doing so would jeopardise its mandatory minimum working balance. This signals tightening in the HRA's financial position and means borrowing is now the primary source of capital funding for housing.
findings.matters: The HRA borrowing requirement is £124.3m by 2026/27 and growing to £140.3m by 2028/29. A constrained revenue position limits the council's ability to absorb loan servicing costs or respond to unexpected pressures, particularly important as HRA borrowing is a material part of total council debt.
findings.figures: HRA CFR growing from £113.609m (2025/26) to £140.307m (2028/29); HRA financing costs rising from 18.0% to 20.1% of HRA revenue
findings.quote: Until 2023/24, the HRA made revenue contributions to the financing of the capital programme. However, this became unsustainable to continue this as it would pose a serious risk to maintaining the HRA minimum working balance.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 16.0% to 22.7% of revenue over three years
findings.detail: The proportion of General Fund revenue consumed by interest and minimum revenue provision (MRP) on borrowing will increase by 6.7 percentage points over the planning period, driven by increased borrowing for capital schemes. This represents a material lock-in of fixed costs from the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Financing costs are a fixed obligation that reduces flexibility to absorb pressures or invest in services. Lenders monitor the proportion of revenue committed to debt servicing as a key sustainability metric.
findings.quote: As can be seen in the above table, the indicators for both the General Fund and the HRA are set to rise over the next three years. This is due to increased borrowing to finance the capital programme, particularly gym equipment replacement, implementation of food waste collections, and fleet vehicle replacements for the General Fund

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing to £174.5m by 2028/29, with HRA debt dominating
findings.detail: The CFR (underlying need to borrow for capital) is rising across the forecast period, from £148.5m to £174.5m. HRA CFR alone grows from £113.6m to £140.3m, driven by the Housing Development Programme, while General Fund CFR remains relatively flat at £34–35m. This signals heavy capital investment in housing over the coming years.
findings.matters: The scale and composition of the CFR tells a lender where the council's capital priorities lie and whether borrowing is concentrated in one service area. The dominance of HRA debt means the council is betting heavily on housing development financing. If HRA finances deteriorate, the council's debt position becomes more exposed.
findings.quote: However, given the Council's extensive Capital Programme, it is inevitable that substantial borrowing will need to take place, particularly for the HRA to finance the Housing Development Programme

findings.headline: £14.3m of loans due for repayment within 12 months from April 2026, with no guarantee of replacement
findings.detail: The council has material refinancing risk: loans totalling £14.3m (including Equal Instalments of Principal) mature within the next 12 months. The strategy explicitly states these 'may not necessarily be replaced with loans of a similar value when they mature' and that replacement will depend on cashflow position at the time.
findings.matters: This refinancing risk is material. The council is not committing to replace this debt, creating uncertainty about whether it will maintain its capital programme funding or face a reduction in borrowing. In a rising interest-rate environment, replacement at current rates will be more expensive.
findings.figures: £14.3m of variable-rate and maturing debt due within 12 months from April 2026; £13.3m repayment due in current year (2025/26)
findings.quote: The Council has loans totalling £14.3m (including EIP instalments) that are due to be repaid within 12 months from April 2026. These loans may not necessarily be replaced with loans of a similar value when they mature and whether or not they are replaced will in part depend upon the cashflow position at the time

findings.headline: Up to £19.0m of new borrowing forecast for 2026/27 to refinance maturing loans and fund capital programme
findings.detail: Council forecasts it will need to raise up to £19.0m in 2026/27, with the explicit purpose of both replacing maturing loans and financing the capital programme. The need for this level of refinancing reflects both the existing debt maturity profile and continued capital investment.
findings.matters: The refinancing requirement shows the council is locked into ongoing borrowing to sustain its capital strategy, with no indication of a planned reduction in external finance. A lender needs to know whether this is a temporary bulge or a structural requirement.
findings.figures: £19.0m forecast new borrowing required in 2026/27
findings.quote: It is forecast that up to £19.0m of new borrowing may be required in 2026/27 to both replace maturing loans due to be repaid and to finance the capital programme

findings.headline: Total debt growing from £95.6m to £123.9m — a 29% increase in one year
findings.detail: Council is expected to hold £123.9m of loans by 31 March 2026, up £15m from 31 March 2025. Fixed-rate debt is rising to £106.7m and variable rate debt to £16.9m. This is part of the strategy for financing capital programmes, particularly HRA housing development.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth changes the council's leverage and debt servicing burden. A lender needs to track whether debt is growing faster than revenue or capital resources can support, and whether the growth is sustainable.
findings.figures: Total Debt: £95.6m (March 2025) → £123.9m (March 2026); fixed-rate PWLB/Market: £87.1m → £106.7m
findings.quote: the Council is expected to hold £123.9m of loans, an increase of £15m when compared to 31 March 2025, as part of the strategy for financing previous years' capital programmes

findings.headline: Investment reserves forecast to fall sharply from £36.9m to £12.0m in four months
findings.detail: Council's investment balance is forecast to drop by £24.9m (67%) between 31 December 2025 and 31 March 2026. The strategy notes that most investments represent revenue reserves, including General Fund and RA working balances. This drawdown is substantial and indicates either acceleration of capital expenditure or operational cash needs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's liquid reserve position and why it is depleting so rapidly. This affects financial resilience and the council's ability to absorb shocks without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Total Investments: £36.9m (31/12/25) → £12.0m (31/03/26 estimate); net movement £24.9m reduction
findings.quote: Total Investments (18,270) (36,898) (12,000)

findings.headline: General Fund budget relies on drawing down £1.2m from reserves in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council proposes withdrawing £760,309 from General Fund Reserve and £439,883 from General Fund earmarked reserves in 2026/27. The document does not explain the reason for this drawdown, its sustainability, or the state of remaining reserves after the withdrawal.
findings.matters: Annual reserve drawdowns to balance budgets indicate an underlying structural deficit that cannot continue indefinitely. Lenders need to understand whether this is a one-off adjustment or part of a pattern that erodes financial resilience.
findings.figures: £760,309 from General Fund Reserve; £439,883 from General Fund earmarked reserves; total £1,200,192
findings.quote: An amount of £760,309 be withdrawn from the General Fund Reserve and an amount of £439,883 be taken from the General Fund earmarked reserves in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: App.2. Forvis Mazars Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Journal authorisation controls are not operating effectively; users are self-authorising transactions inappropriately.
findings.detail: Testing identified users who self-authorised journal entries when they should not have been able to, and one user without formal authorisation rights was able to post and self-authorise a journal with no review mechanism. While extended testing found no actual errors, the control weakness creates material fraud risk. Management has agreed to implement a full review of access rights.
findings.matters: Journal authorisation is a critical control to prevent errors and fraud in financial reporting. Users able to override controls without review represents a control deficiency with fraud implications.
findings.figures: No errors found in extended testing, but deficiency affected internal finance team journal transfers
findings.quote: During our testing of journals, we identified certain users that had self-authorised journal entries when they should not have. We extended our testing with no issues arising. Additionally, we identified an instance where a user who does not have formal authorisation rights in the system was able to post and self-authorise a journal without any review mechanism in place.

findings.paper_title: App.2. Forvis Mazars Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision calculations do not comply with the council's stated policy or accounting standards.
findings.detail: The council uses asset lives in MRP calculations that do not align with those in the asset register and depreciation schedules, resulting in an undercharge of £119,000. Additionally, the Housing Revenue Account makes no voluntary revenue provision for debt repayment. Management has agreed to undertake a full review of MRP calculations during budget setting.
findings.matters: MRP is how councils plan repayment of borrowing. Errors in this calculation indicate uncertainty about whether debt repayment capacity is being properly assessed.
findings.figures: £119,000 MRP undercharge; asset lives inconsistency between MRP and depreciation calculations
findings.quote: The Council has not fully adhered to its formal MRP Policy. While adopting Option 3 – Asset Life Method under statutory guidance, the asset lives used in MRP calculations do not align with those recorded in the asset register and applied for depreciation.

findings.paper_title: App.2. Forvis Mazars Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The asset valuation process lacked adequate controls, with incomplete instructions and errors not being detected.
findings.detail: The council gave incomplete instructions to its external valuer, omitting certain benchmark assets. When the external valuer made a significant input error, the council failed to identify it during review. The internal valuation process also experienced significant delays that compressed the time available for quality assurance and review procedures.
findings.matters: Asset valuations are fundamental to the balance sheet and financial position. Failure to catch valuation errors indicates inadequate review processes for major balance sheet items.
findings.figures: £43.6 million in dwelling valuation errors; £371,000 in car park valuation errors identified
findings.quote: The Council's asset valuation process lacked adequate controls, as instructions to the external valuer of Council dwellings omitted certain beacon assets and the Council failed to identify a significant input error by the external valuer when recording the results of the valuation.

findings.paper_title: App.2. Forvis Mazars Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant control deficiencies exist throughout the capital accounting framework.
findings.detail: The auditors identified systematic control failures in how the council records capital transactions: discrepancies between the Fixed Asset Register and general ledger, incorrect disposal calculations, failure to clear revaluation reserves, misclassification of transactions, and inconsistent application of accounting standards. Management acknowledged these arose from timing pressures and committed to earlier scheduling of valuations.
findings.matters: These are systemic control failures affecting the entire capital accounting process, not isolated errors, indicating fundamental weaknesses in the council's financial management systems.
findings.figures: Multiple errors across several categories; adjusted misstatements in capital accounting exceeded £2.5 million
findings.quote: During the audit, we identified a significant deficiency in the Council's capital accounting processes, evidenced by multiple issues including discrepancies between the Fixed Asset Register and the general ledger, incorrect calculation and posting of asset disposals, failure to clear revaluation reserve balances, misclassification of capital transactions, and inconsistent application of CIPFA Code requirements for statutory adjustments.

findings.paper_title: App.2. Forvis Mazars Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The council's valuation of council dwellings was materially misstated, requiring a £43.6 million downward adjustment.
findings.detail: The audit identified multiple cumulative errors in the valuation of council dwellings, including using benchmark values from 2022 instead of 2024, counting an incorrect number of dwellings, and calculation errors. This single adjustment was approximately 29 times the overall materiality threshold. Management acknowledged the root cause as late completion of asset valuations that compressed time for quality assurance.
findings.matters: This demonstrates serious control weaknesses in managing the council's largest asset class and raises questions about balance sheet reliability and asset management capability.
findings.figures: £43,618,000 adjustment; overall materiality £1,480,000
findings.quote: Due to cumulative impact of a number of errors in the valuation of council dwellings. This is a net reduction in the value of Council dwellings.

findings.headline: Auditors found £633k of material misstatements that management chose not to correct in the accounts
findings.detail: The auditors identified three material errors in Broxtowe's 2024/25 financial statements: a £119k undercharge in Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) affecting the council's debt repayment calculation, a £143k pension fund asset valuation error found by the pension auditor, and a £371k error in the car park valuation methodology. Management decided to leave all three uncorrected, having consulted the Governance, Audit and Standards Committee and judging them immaterial in aggregate.
findings.matters: Unadjusted audit misstatements indicate control weaknesses in financial accounting. The MRP undercharge is particularly concerning for a lender because it directly affects the accuracy of the council's debt repayment obligations—material information for credit assessment. Material errors left uncorrected suggest the council's internal controls over financial reporting may not be operating reliably.
findings.figures: £119k, £143k, £371k, £633k aggregate
findings.quote: The Council's management, following consultation with the Chair of the Governance, Audit and Standards Committee, decided not to adjust the Statement of Accounts for the following items on the grounds of materiality.

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Journal authorization control failure allowing unauthorized users to post and approve entries
findings.detail: Auditors identified 'an instance where a user who does not have formal authorisation rights in the system was able to post and self-authorise a journal without any review mechanism in place.' A full review of general ledger access rights has now been undertaken.
findings.matters: Breakdown of journal authorization controls creates direct fraud risk and material misstatement risk in the general ledger, particularly concerning given concurrent capital accounting control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Additionally, we identified an instance where a user who does not have formal authorisation rights in the system was able to post and self-authorise a journal without any review mechanism in place.

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital receipts reserve depleted 25% year-on-year, limiting flexibility for capital investment
findings.detail: Capital Receipts Reserve fell from £6.3m to £4.7m in 2024/25, a £1.6m reduction. Capital expenditure for the year was £31.4m. With reserves depleting and a £7.2m medium-term funding gap, capital programme flexibility is increasingly constrained.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a discretionary funding source; their depletion restricts future capital investment and often forces reliance on external borrowing or grant funding, both increasingly difficult for financially stressed councils.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts Reserve £4.7m (down from £6.3m); capital expenditure £31.4m in 2024/25
findings.quote: the Capital Receipts Reserve of £4.7m, down from £6.3m in 2023/24 in line with the funding of capital expenditure

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Chief Executive retirement and interim replacement during period of financial stress and organisational change
findings.detail: The previous Chief Executive retired and was replaced with an interim from existing senior management. While auditors note this 'ensured continuity in understanding', the change occurs during a critical period: widening budget deficits, LGR uncertainty, capital control issues, and reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Leadership continuity is material when a council faces structural deficits and existential reorganisation. Interim arrangements limit decision-making authority and experience during critical planning cycles.
findings.figures: Not provided
findings.quote: There have been recent changes in management arrangements following the retirement of the previous Chief Executive. The interim replacement and other changes that have been made as a consequence have utilised existing senior management, ensuring continuity in understanding of the Council and its plans.

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates material governance and planning uncertainty, with council opposing both proposed outcomes
findings.detail: Government proposals would merge Broxtowe with Nottingham City under two options; the council 'does not currently support either of these options' but must plan for 2028 implementation. Auditors identify transition risks including 'financial risks and sustainability, including transitional costs, plans to bridge budget gaps and the impact to the capital programme.'
findings.matters: Forced local government reorganisation creates planning uncertainty, transition costs, and risk to capital programme delivery during a period when the council already faces a widening structural budget deficit.
findings.figures: Implementation target April 2028; further LGR announcements expected winter 2025
findings.quote: The future uncertainty presents a significant challenge for the Council. The Council can only ensure that it continues to act responsibly, continues to deliver its services for local people and performs its other duties until reorganisation is complete

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant deficiencies in capital accounting controls and asset valuation processes requiring multiple audit adjustments
findings.detail: Auditors identified multiple control weaknesses including discrepancies between the Fixed Asset Register and general ledger, incorrect disposal calculations, incomplete instructions to external valuers, and failure to identify significant valuation errors. A £371k error in car park valuation methodology and a £119k MRP undercharge were not corrected. The audit notes 'late completion of asset valuations compromised the time available' for quality review.
findings.matters: Systemic weaknesses in capital accounting and asset valuation processes indicate inadequate financial controls and create risk of undetected misstatement in material balance sheet items.
findings.figures: £371k uncorrected error in car park valuation; £119k MRP undercharge; £143k pension asset understatement; total uncorrected misstatements £633k
findings.quote: we identified a significant deficiency in the Council's capital accounting processes, evidenced by multiple issues including discrepancies between the Fixed Asset Register and the general ledger, incorrect calculation and posting of asset disposals, failure to clear revaluation reserve balances, misclassification of capital transactions

findings.paper_title: App.3 Forvis Mazars Draft Auditors Audit Report 2024-25
findings.headline: General fund reserves will be depleted by end of 2027/28 with no funding solution identified yet
findings.detail: The MTFS shows the general fund working balance is projected to be completely depleted by 2027/28, the last year covered in the strategy. The council's useable reserves fell from £18.3m to £15.6m in 2024/25. Auditors note the council is 'actively reviewing its financial strategy' but there is 'an increasing need to identify, agree and implement a plan to close the widening financial gap.'
findings.matters: A council with depleting reserves that cannot guarantee a funded medium-term financial plan represents deteriorating credit strength and operational risk.
findings.figures: General fund and earmarked reserves £8.6m (down from £8.8m); reserves projected to zero by 2027/28; shortfall of £7.2m from 2025/26 through 2028/29
findings.quote: the general fund working balance is estimated to be completely depleted by the end of 2027/28, being the last year in MTFS; The Council is actively reviewing its financial strategy to address this shortfall and ensure long-term sustainability

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: High priority stores procedure documentation delayed five months past original deadline
findings.detail: Production of appropriate and up-to-date procedural documents for stores management was originally due 31 July 2025. As of this report, initial drafting exists but further work remains, with revised completion target now 31 December 2025. Management acknowledge the development has taken longer than anticipated.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-priority audit recommendations indicate control weaknesses in purchasing and inventory management. Delays in implementing remedial actions suggest audit findings are not receiving adequate management attention.
findings.figures: Original target: 31 July 2025; Revised target: 31 December 2025
findings.quote: It is acknowledged that the development of processes has taken longer than initially anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: High priority damp and mould procurement action delayed one full year to March 2026
findings.detail: The high-priority action to complete procurement for damp and mould remediation works was originally due 31 March 2025 but remains in progress. The revised target is now 31 March 2026. Management report that repair contracts are being prioritized by highest value, which may indicate resource or budgetary constraints affecting delivery.
findings.matters: Delays in remediating damp and mould in council housing increase maintenance costs, tenant disputes, and reputational damage. A full year delay on a high-priority remediation program signals either capacity constraints or deprioritization of housing asset maintenance.
findings.figures: Original target: 31 March 2025; Revised target: 31 March 2026
findings.quote: This is still in progress. The Repairs team have a number of contracts requiring procurement and have prioritised those with the highest value.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Financial Performance Management Update
findings.headline: Major cremator replacement capital project shows £50.5k overspend but is expected to settle within revised projection
findings.detail: The cremator replacement project (including £1.34m brought forward from 2024/25) has committed spend of £1,389,527 against a revised budget of £1,339,050. However, the projection is £1,334,000, indicating the committee expects final costs to resolve below the revised estimate once outstanding purchase orders close and final invoices are received.
findings.matters: Large capital projects reveal cost management discipline; this project required significant brought-forward funding which may indicate cash flow pressures
findings.figures: Revised budget £1,339,050; actual/committed £1,389,527; overspend £50,477; latest projection £1,334,000
findings.quote: The commitments figure will be £55k lower once outstanding purchase order has been closed and final invoice received.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Financial Performance Management Update
findings.headline: Memorialisation income forecast £20.6k lower due to the same competitive market pressures affecting cremation fees
findings.detail: Memorialisation income (visual tributes, book of remembrance) is budgeted at £133,600 but projected to deliver only £113,000. The same competitive market and fewer bookings affecting cremation fees are also reducing this secondary revenue stream.
findings.matters: Multiple revenue lines affected by competitive pressure reinforces the seriousness of the market challenge facing the service
findings.figures: Budget £133,600; projected £113,000; variance £20,600
findings.quote: Outturn anticipated to be less due to competitive market with less bookings being received.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Financial Performance Management Update
findings.headline: Medical referee fees projected at £45k, more than double the £20k budget, due to regulatory cost pressures
findings.detail: The committee budgeted £20,000 for medical referee fees but projects spending £45,000 for the full year. Although government has postponed the start date of new medical referee fee rules, the committee expects costs to remain at levels similar to the previous year.
findings.matters: A significant and unexpected cost increase from regulatory requirements that may signal wider cost pressures on councils if this regulation applies broadly
findings.figures: Budget £20,000; projected £45,000; variance £25,000
findings.quote: Government has postponed the start date on medical referee fee rules, so costs expected to be similar to the previous year.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Financial Performance Management Update
findings.headline: Cremation fee income projected to fall by £148.8k (6.6%) due to fewer bookings in a competitive market
findings.detail: The joint committee budgeted £2,263,800 for cremation fee income but now projects £2,115,000 for the full year. The shortfall reflects competitive market pressures resulting in fewer bookings being received, as noted in the committee's commentary.
findings.matters: Revenue decline from competitive pressure is an early warning sign for lenders about market demand and competitive positioning of the service
findings.figures: Budget £2,263,800; projected £2,115,000; variance £148,800
findings.quote: Outturn anticipated to be less due to competitive market with less bookings being received – see separate Performance and Marketing report.

news_drafts.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £67k if 3.3% uplift accepted against 3% budget assumption
news_drafts.lead: Unbudgeted pay inflation is a direct hit to the bottom line with no mitigation identified; represents unfunded cost pressure.

news_drafts.headline: Stapleford Towns Fund street improvement scheme flagged with explicit budget risk to completion
news_drafts.lead: Acknowledged budget risk on externally-funded scheme affects council's ability to deliver town regeneration commitments within available funding.

news_drafts.headline: Housing structural repairs budget at risk due to legacy issues and case volumes
news_drafts.lead: Structural defects are not discretionary spending; unbudgeted costs cannot be deferred and may force reductions elsewhere.
